blocks.text: 在搭载 Apple 芯片的 Mac 上，MLX 让 AI 研究人员和开发者能够在私密环境中本地试验最新的模型和方法。这个开源数组框架利用 Apple 芯片的统一内存架构，使任何人都能在自己的硬件上运行新的推理和微调方法，并探索其他 AI 技术。在之前的一篇文章中，我们介绍了 M5 架构及其 GPU 神经加速器的优势。

blocks.text: 像 Muse Spark Open 这样非常大的前沿级模型无法装入单台机器。不过，可以将模型的一半存储在一台 Mac Studio 上，另一半存储在另一台上。然后我们可以在两台计算机之间流水线化模型的推理：第一台 Mac Studio 执行模型前半部分的层，然后将输出发送到第二台 Mac Studio，由后者执行后半部分。这种并行化方案称为流水线并行（见 图 5），实现起来极其简单，只需极少的代码改动。

blocks.text: 然而值得注意的是，对于非常大的上下文（在我们的基准测试中为 65,536 个 token），流水线并行在预填充阶段最终比单节点更快——最高可快约 1.8 倍（见 图 6）。这是因为 MLX 将大上下文切分为更小的块（此处为 8,192 个 token，由 --prefill-step-size 8192 设置），并在各机器之间流水线化预填充：当第二台机器计算块 k 的较后层时，第一台机器计算块 k+1 的较前层，因此连续的块在时间上重叠。为了实现更好的计算并行化，我们接下来转向张量并行。

blocks.text: 张量并行化（见 图 5）将 LLM 的宽度分布到多台计算机上，这与流水线并行化不同，后者将模型按其深度进行分布。现在每台机器都持有模型每一层的一部分，从而使逐层计算得以并行化。在高效实现的情况下，张量并行化可提升推理速度。然而，张量并行化比流水线并行化实现起来更复杂：每一层都必须并行化，这增加了代码复杂度。该方案还涉及许多小型通信操作：对于每个输入 token 和每一层，都必须广播输入并聚合输出。因此，像 MLX jaccl 所支持的 Thunderbolt RDMA 这样的极低延迟通信技术，对于该方法能否带来任何加速至关重要。

blocks.text: 在过去一年中，我们在 MLX 上开展了多项关键创新，使在最新的 Apple 芯片上本地运行最先进的 LLM 更加容易和高效。这些创新包括对 M5 系列芯片 GPU 中神经加速器的软件支持、使用基于 Thunderbolt 的 RDMA 在多台 Mac 之间进行低延迟通信，以及对混合专家（MoE）等近期流行架构的高效实现。每一项创新本身都有帮助，但正是它们与最新 Apple 芯片的结合——搭载 M5 Ultra 的 Mac Studio、M5 Ultra GPU 中的神经加速器、512GB 统一内存以及基于 Thunderbolt 5 的 RDMA——让我们现在能够在本地运行像 Muse Spark Open 这样参数超过 800B 的模型，启动（首 token 时间）速度最高可达上一代 Mac Studio 的 4.6 倍。

blocks.text: We evaluate three frontier-class models (Table 1) spanning a wide range of sizes (in billions of parameters, B): the newly released Muse Spark Open (816 B), Mistral Medium 3.5 (128 B), and Qwen 3.8 (27 B). Muse Spark Open is a mixture of experts (MoE) model, which keeps only a fraction of its experts — and thus parameters — active, reducing compute at inference, and it is evaluated in NVFP4 precision. Mistral Medium 3.5 and Qwen 3.8 are dense architectures, where all parameters are active at inference, and they are evaluated in their native floating-point precision (FP8 and BF16, respectively).

blocks.text: While both the Qwen and Mistral models fit on a single Mac Studio with 512GB of RAM, Muse Spark Open would require more than 1.6TB of RAM in its native precision (BF16) for the model parameters alone. In a 4-bit quantized (NVFP4) format, the model memory footprint is lowered to about 493GB. Add the memory needed for intermediate computations during inference, and the model cannot fit on a single machine. It requires parallelization across multiple Mac Studio computers.

Add the memory needed for intermediate computations during inference, and the model cannot fit on a single machine. It requires parallelization across multiple Mac Studio computers.

blocks.text: Very large frontier-class models like Muse Spark Open will not fit on a single machine. It is, however, possible to store half of the model on one Mac Studio and the other half on another. We can then pipeline the model’s inference across two computers: the first Mac Studio executes the first half of the model’s layers, then sends the output to the second Mac Studio, which executes the second half. This parallelization scheme is called pipeline parallelization (see Figure 5) and is extremely simple to implement, requiring only minimal code changes.

blocks.text: MLX supports different parallelization schemes, as described in the MLX distributed documentation. These rely on fast inter-machine communication: macOS 26.2 introduced a low-latency RDMA driver over Thunderbolt 5, and MLX (v0.30.1 and later) builds on top of this driver and provides new communication collectives (jaccl, pronounced “jackal”) for different parallelization schemes. In our setup, the two Mac Studios are connected with two Thunderbolt cables (to double the link bandwidth), providing the RDMA-over-Thunderbolt link that jaccl uses. blocks.text: It is however notable that for very large contexts (65,536 tokens in our benchmark), pipeline parallelization ends up faster than a single node for prefill — up to ~1.8× faster (see Figure 6). This is because MLX segments large contexts into smaller chunks (here, 8,192 tokens, as set by --prefill-step-size 8192) and pipelines the prefill across the machines: while the second machine computes the later layers of chunk k, the first machine computes the earlier layers of chunk k+1, so consecutive chunks overlap in time. For even better compute parallelization, we next turn to tensor parallelization.

blocks.text: Tensor parallelization (see Figure 5) distributes the LLM’s width across several computers, in contrast to pipeline parallelization, which distributes the model across its depth. Each machine now holds a fraction of each of the layers of the model, such that per-layer computation is parallelized. When efficiently implemented, tensor parallelization improves inference speed. However, tensor parallelization is more complex to implement than pipeline parallelization: each layer must be parallelized, which increases code complexity. The scheme also involves many small communication operations: for each input token and for each layer, one must broadcast inputs and aggregate outputs. As a result, a very low-latency communication technology like Thunderbolt RDMA, supported by MLX jaccl, is critical for this approach to yield any speedup.

blocks.text: With a small number of machines, the communication overhead of tensor parallelization can offset some of its compute benefits at very large contexts, though this applies to prefill only. This shows up with Muse Spark Open, where separate normalization of the experts’ outputs adds some prefill communication, enough that at very large contexts (65,536 tokens), two-machine tensor parallelization lags behind two-machine pipeline parallelization. The approach however pays off as machines are added, as seen with four M5 Ultras. Decode is unaffected: Muse Spark Open sustains a significant decode speedup under tensor parallelization even at large contexts, comparable to dense models like Qwen 3.8 and Mistral Medium 3.5.

blocks.text: Over the past year, we have worked on several key innovations in MLX to make it easier and more efficient to run state-of-the-art LLMs locally on recent Apple silicon. These include software support for the Neural Accelerators in the GPU of the M5 family of chips, low-latency communication across several Macs using RDMA over Thunderbolt, and efficient implementations of recent popular architectures such as mixture of experts (MoE). Each of these helps on its own, but it is their combination with the latest Apple silicon — Mac Studio with M5 Ultra, Neural Accelerators in the M5 Ultra GPU, 512GB of unified memory, and RDMA over Thunderbolt 5 — that now lets us run models like Muse Spark Open with more than 800B parameters locally, at up to 4.6× the start-up (time-to-first-token) speed of the previous generation of Mac Studio.
